summary: All 22 units were read in full and every numeric, MCQ and localisation key was worked independently. The content is of high quality. Cerebellar double decussation, the direct/indirect basal ganglia circuit, spinothalamic and dorsal column crossing (including the Brown-Sequard items), Weber/Wallenberg/medial medullary localisation, uvula deviation, third-nerve pupil involvement, RLN course, lenticulostriate lacunar stroke and PCA macular sparing are all correct and internally consistent, and all localisation questions have a single defensible answer. One major error was found (a marking guide that wrongly includes sternocleidomastoid weakness after posterior-triangle accessory nerve injury) plus a few minor precision issues. This is an AI review only: the course still needs a subject-matter expert before clinical reliance.

issues.problem: Marking guide: "Accessory nerve injury causes weakness of trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, shoulder droop and inability to shrug". The question is about surgery in the posterior triangle. There the accessory nerve has already given its branch to sternocleidomastoid, so injury causes trapezius weakness only (drooping shoulder, winged scapula, cannot shrug). The lesson hook and the explanation describe trapezius-only signs, so the guide contradicts them and would teach a wrong localisation.
issues.suggestedFix: Change to: accessory nerve injury in the posterior triangle weakens trapezius (shoulder droop, scapular winging, weak shrug); sternocleidomastoid is usually spared because its branch leaves the nerve higher up.

issues.problem: Lesson gives AHI bands as "mild at 5-15, moderate at 15-30 and severe above 30". The bands overlap at 15 and 30, and normal (<5) is not stated. The keyed question (AHI 24) is unaffected.
issues.suggestedFix: State the bands as normal <5, mild 5 to <15, moderate 15 to 30, severe >30 events per hour.

issues.problem: Pons worked example attributes an isolated ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy to the "abducens nucleus" and facial fascicle in the caudal pontine tegmentum. A nuclear abducens lesion gives an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy, not an isolated abduction failure. An isolated lateral rectus palsy with facial weakness and contralateral hemiparesis (Millard-Gubler) reflects a fascicular lesion in the ventral pons.
issues.suggestedFix: Say the abducens and facial nerve fascicles (not the nucleus) are damaged as they pass through the ventral caudal pons, and name the pattern as Millard-Gubler. Optionally note that a nuclear lesion gives gaze palsy.

issues.problem: Key and explanation say cardiac afferents converge with arm input on the same cord segments and so refer pain to "the arm and jaw". Jaw referral is not explained by T1-T4 dorsal horn convergence; it is attributed to convergence of vagal and cervical afferents with trigeminal input in the brainstem and upper cervical cord.
issues.suggestedFix: Keep option a as the key. Amend the explanation so the arm is explained by T1-T4 convergence and the jaw by brainstem/upper cervical convergence.

issues.problem: Lesson and explanation state that lenticulostriate (MCA) branches supply the internal capsule. The posterior limb and lower capsule also receive supply from the anterior choroidal artery (an ICA branch), and the ACA recurrent artery of Heubner supplies the anterior limb. The key remains the only defensible option, but the lesson is a slight oversimplification.
issues.suggestedFix: Add one sentence noting the anterior choroidal artery supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, and that lacunes arise from small penetrating arteries more generally.
